newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope leaves hospital under "orders" to rest.
newsitem.headline: Pope leaves hospital under "orders" to rest.

text.p: Pope John Paul left hospital on Tuesday one week after an operation to remove his appendix and with no sign that he will obey doctors' orders to slow down.
"This is a happy day because he is returning home cured," Professor Francesco Crucitti told reporters minutes after the 76-year-old Pope left the Gemelli Hospital for the Vatican.
Crucitti led the team of surgeons who operated on the Pope to remove his appendix last Tuesday. The operation confirmed that there was no recurrence of a colon tumour removed in 1992.
Crucitti said doctors had not set a specific amount of time for the Pope to rest.
"But we told him he had to rest," Crucitti said firmly.
Asked if he believed the Pope would obey the orders, Crucitti smiled and said: "Ah, now that remains to be seen."
Crucitti, who accompanied the Pope through the lobby of the hospital to his waiting limousine, said he was convinced that the Pontiff would make a full recovery.
"Yes, he had an operation but it was a small operation of modest dimensions," Crucitti said, adding that he expected to visit the Pope at least once at the Vatican.
The surgeon described the Pope as "certainly in good shape" and added: "He has overcome this illness and this operation like any other patient in good condition would."
The Pope, who had his stitches removed on Tuesday morning, walked slowly through the lobby of the hospital. He used a cane at first but then passed it to one of his aides.
The Pope's next public appearance is due on Sunday, when he will recite his weekly prayer and address from the window of his apartments overlooking St Peter's Square.

The Vatican has not excluded the possibility that the Pope will make a brief appearance from the window on Wednesday, the 18th anniversary of his election in 1978 as the first non-Italian Pope in 455 years.
The Pope entered the Gemelli on October 6 for the sixth time since his election after doctors diagnosed an inflamed appendix as the cause of bouts of fever and abdominal pain.
The first time was for life-saving surgery in 1981 after Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca shot him in St Peter's Square.
The Pope on Sunday jokingly called the Gemelli "Vatican Three" after St Peter's and his summer residence.
Before leaving he comforted children suffering from cancer, some of them terminally ill, in the cancer ward next to his 10th floor suite.
The young patients had sent the Pope a note, signed "the children next door", asking him to visit before he left.
